messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forensic Analyst
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
  Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Vignette:
The assault happened in the forensic lab where she had worked for thirty-two years. It was late, past midnight, during a rush on a cold-case review. Eleanor was alone, cross-referencing bone-fracture patterns against old autopsy photographs, when a colleague she had trusted—a man twenty years her junior—cornered her by the evidence lockers. He did not strike her. He did not need to. What he did was place his hand flat against her throat, pin her against the steel doors, and whisper exactly what he would do if she ever told anyone about the discrepancy she had found in his case files. The pressure of his palm against her larynx, the cold metal through her thin blouse, his wedding ring pressing into her windpipe—those sensations had burned themselves into her body. She did not report it. She told herself the threat was empty, that she could manage him, that she was a professional. She finished the shift. She went home. She did not tell her husband.

In the weeks that followed, Eleanor began to notice that her body felt like a trap. When her husband, Martin, mentioned their upcoming fortieth anniversary cruise—a trip they had saved for years to take—she felt something detonate in her chest. Talking about the future had become unbearable. Every plan, every calendar date, every mention of “next year” landed on her like a physical weight. She would go quiet, stare at her hands, and change the subject. Martin assumed she was tired. She let him believe that.

The memory of the assault would not stay still. Sometimes it arrived in fragments—the gleam of the lockers, the pressure of the ring—but before she could reach the end, something in her mind would fling the door shut. She would be left with a slammed-door feeling, her heart racing, the story unfinished. At other times, the memory came complete but hollow: she could see the scene, hear his voice, feel the cold metal, yet she felt nothing at all. It was as if she were watching a woman who looked like her being attacked in a documentary. That numbness frightened her more than the rage did, and the rage was considerable. When the full memory broke through—when she could not block it fast enough—she felt a fury so pure and so hot that she had to grip the kitchen counter to keep from breaking something. She had never been an angry person. She did not know what to do with this stranger inside her.

She began to believe that she was inadequate. The thought arrived fully formed one morning as she stood in front of the bathroom mirror, her hand touching her own throat. A woman who could not defend herself, who could not report what happened, who could not even hold a coherent memory of the event—that woman was not the person she had been. She had been happy once. She remembered that the way one remembers a foreign country visited long ago. Now she woke miserable, and the misery had become the background hum of her life.

Her strategies for survival were precise and, in their way, logical. She stopped exercising entirely. The local gym had a row of treadmills facing a mirrored wall, and the sight of a man’s forearm—the same width, the same watch—had sent her fleeing mid-stride three months ago. She never went back. At home, she began to sit only in chairs that allowed her to place her back against a wall, her eyes scanning the room. In restaurants, she chose the corner booth. In the lab, she rearranged her workstation so that her chair faced the door, her spine pressed against the filing cabinets. She told herself she was being practical. She was not. She was terrified.

Eating became a negotiation. She could manage a few bites of toast in the morning if she ate alone. Dinner with Martin was harder—she would push food around her plate, claim she had eaten a late lunch, and retreat to the bedroom. She had lost twelve pounds. Her clothes hung loose. Martin had started to ask, gently, if she was ill. She said she was fine.

What finally brought her to seek help was not the weight loss or the sleeplessness or the rage. It was a single moment in the lab, three weeks ago, when a junior analyst asked her opinion on a case file. The file involved a cold-case assault. Eleanor opened the folder, saw the crime-scene photographs, and felt her mind go blank. She could not speak. She sat there, her back against the wall, her hand pressed to her throat, while the young woman waited for an answer. Eleanor excused herself, walked to the bathroom, and locked the door. She stood there for twenty minutes, staring at her own reflection, and for the first time she thought: I cannot do this alone.

She is afraid that therapy will make it worse. She is afraid that if she lets herself fully remember, she will not come back. But she is more afraid of the life she is living now—the small rooms, the empty plates, the future she cannot bear to name. She came here because she wants to believe that the woman who was happy still exists somewhere, and that maybe, if someone helps her open the door, she will find her still alive.
